nodes.name: Artificial neuron
nodes.statement: An artificial neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, z = Σ wᵢxᵢ + b. It then passes z through an activation function.

nodes.name: Activation function
nodes.statement: An activation function is a fixed nonlinear function applied to each weighted sum. Common choices are ReLU(z) = max(0, z) and the sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1 + e⁻ᶻ).

nodes.name: Layer as matrix product
nodes.statement: A layer computes all its neurons at once as h = f(Wx + b). Row i of the matrix W holds the weights of neuron i.

nodes.name: Network as composition
nodes.statement: A feedforward network feeds each layer's output into the next layer. Its output is a nested function such as f₂(W₂ f₁(W₁x + b₁) + b₂).

nodes.name: Linear layers collapse
nodes.statement: Without activations, two layers give W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x, which is a single linear map. Stacking more linear layers then adds no expressive power.

nodes.name: XOR is not linear
nodes.statement: No straight line separates the XOR points (0,1) and (1,0) from (0,0) and (1,1). So a single linear neuron cannot compute XOR.

nodes.name: Nonlinearity is required
nodes.statement: A network can represent curved decision boundaries, such as the one XOR needs, only because its activations are nonlinear.

nodes.name: Hidden layer solves XOR
nodes.statement: A network with one hidden layer of two ReLU units can compute XOR. The hidden units remap the four inputs into a space where the two classes are linearly separable.

nodes.name: Universal approximation
nodes.statement: A network with one hidden layer and enough nonlinear units can approximate any continuous function on a closed, bounded region to any desired accuracy.

nodes.name: Loss function
nodes.statement: A loss compares the network's output with the target and returns one number. Squared error (ŷ − y)² is common for regression, and cross-entropy −log p(correct class) for classification.

nodes.name: Softmax outputs
nodes.statement: Softmax turns a vector of scores zₖ into probabilities pₖ = exp(zₖ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ). The results are positive and sum to 1.

nodes.name: Training is optimization
nodes.statement: Training adjusts all weights and biases to minimize the average loss over the training examples.

nodes.name: Gradient descent step
nodes.statement: Gradient descent updates each weight by w ← w − α ∂L/∂w. This moves the weight a small amount in the direction that lowers the loss.

nodes.name: Chain rule
nodes.statement: If the loss L depends on a weight w only through an intermediate value z, then ∂L/∂w = (∂L/∂z)(∂z/∂w).

nodes.name: Local derivatives
nodes.statement: Each operation in a network has a simple local derivative. For z = wx + b, ∂z/∂w = x and ∂z/∂b = 1, and ReLU has derivative 1 for z > 0 and 0 for z < 0.

nodes.name: Backpropagation algorithm
nodes.statement: Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss backward through the network, one layer at a time. Each layer reuses the gradient already computed for the layer above it.

nodes.name: Cost of backprop
nodes.statement: One backward pass costs a small constant multiple of one forward pass, about two to three times, however many weights the network has. So the gradient for every weight comes almost as cheaply as one prediction.

nodes.name: Forward pass cache
nodes.statement: The backward pass needs the inputs and weighted sums stored during the forward pass. This is why training uses much more memory than prediction alone.

nodes.name: Weight gradient as outer product
nodes.statement: For a layer z = Wx + b, the gradient ∂L/∂W is the outer product of the upstream gradient ∂L/∂z with the input x. The bias gradient ∂L/∂b is ∂L/∂z itself.

nodes.name: Softmax cross-entropy gradient
nodes.statement: When softmax is followed by cross-entropy, the gradient of the loss with respect to the scores is p − y. That is the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot target.

nodes.name: Symmetry breaking
nodes.statement: If all neurons in a layer start with equal weights, they receive equal gradients and stay identical forever. Random initialization breaks this symmetry so that each neuron can learn a different feature.

nodes.name: Sigmoid saturates
nodes.statement: The sigmoid's derivative σ(z)(1 − σ(z)) is at most 0.25. It approaches 0 when |z| is large.

nodes.name: Vanishing gradients
nodes.statement: The gradient reaching an early layer is a product of one local derivative per later layer. When those factors are below 1, the gradient shrinks exponentially with depth.

nodes.name: ReLU keeps gradients alive
nodes.statement: ReLU has derivative exactly 1 for positive inputs. So gradients pass through the active units of many layers without shrinking.

nodes.name: Initialization scale
nodes.statement: Drawing a ReLU layer's weights with variance 2/n, where n is the number of inputs to the layer, keeps the size of the activations roughly constant from layer to layer. This scheme is called He initialization.

nodes.name: Overfitting to training data
nodes.statement: A network with enough parameters can memorize its training set. It then reaches a low training loss but a high loss on new data.

nodes.name: Validation set
nodes.statement: Loss measured on held-out examples estimates performance on new data. It reveals overfitting that the training loss hides.

nodes.name: Weight decay
nodes.statement: Adding λ‖w‖² to the loss pulls every weight toward zero at each step. This favours smoother functions and reduces overfitting.
